lead: A browser turns HTML, CSS and JavaScript into a screen you can use. A web server answers requests for files. An application server runs the code that decides, calculates and saves data. These three roles appear in every web system, from an IRCTC ticket page to a UPI payment screen. The roles are separate ideas, but one machine or one process can play more than one role. This chapter shows what each part does and how a request moves through them.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for client, server and tiers.

sections.h3: Browser parts and the request path

blocks.text: A browser is a program that fetches web resources and renders them. It has four parts you should name. The rendering engine turns HTML and CSS into pixels; examples are Blink in Chrome and Edge, Gecko in Firefox, WebKit in Safari. The JavaScript engine runs scripts; examples are V8 in Chrome and Node.js, SpiderMonkey in Firefox. The network stack opens connections and sends HTTP requests; HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, the encryption layer. Storage keeps cookies in small key-value records and localStorage in larger key-value records; both survive page reloads. The same-origin policy lets a page read storage and responses only from the same protocol, host and port, unless the server allows otherwise.

When you type a URL, DNS gives an IP address (see 1.1), the network stack connects to the server, and the browser asks for the page. HTTP details are in 1.4. The response may come from a web server as a stored file, or from an application server as computed output. The browser does not know which one produced it; it only reads status codes, headers and body.

sections.h3: Web server: files, TLS and reverse proxy

blocks.text: A web server is software that listens on a port, accepts connections, reads an HTTP request, and sends a response. Apache HTTP Server and Nginx are common. Public web servers listen on port 80 for HTTP and port 443 for HTTPS; port numbers are part of the address. A static request asks for a file that already exists: /logo.png, /style.css, /index.html. The web server reads the file from disk and returns it with a content type. This is fast because no program runs per request beyond the server itself.

On HTTPS, the web server often ends TLS: it decrypts the request and encrypts the response. It can also act as a reverse proxy. A reverse proxy accepts requests from clients and forwards them to another server, usually on an internal port such as 3000 for a Node.js app or 8080 for Tomcat. Clients see one public address; the back-end ports stay private. Nginx may serve 700 static requests per minute and proxy 300 requests per minute to an Express app. A dynamic request needs code to run: read a form, check a login, query a database. The web server forwards it; the application server handles it.

sections.h3: Application server, middleware and request lifecycle

blocks.text: An application server runs application code for dynamic requests. It may be a Java process in Tomcat, a Node.js process running Express, or a Python process running Django. It loads routes, runs handlers, talks to a database, and builds a response. In small systems the same Node.js process can serve static files and run app code; the roles are roles, not always separate machines.

Middleware is code that runs between the request and the final handler. It can log a request, parse JSON, check a session cookie, add CORS headers, or reject a bad request. Express calls these functions middleware; Java servlet filters do similar work. Some syllabi call the application server the middleware host because middleware runs inside it.

Request lifecycle: 1 accept the TCP connection; 2 read and parse the HTTP request; 3 route by method and path; 4 run middleware; 5 run the handler and database queries; 6 build status, headers and body; 7 send the response; 8 log and close or reuse the connection. A web server does steps 1-2 and then either serves a file or forwards to an app server. The app server does 3-7. Logging can happen in both. If the database is slow, the handler waits; the server must handle other requests in parallel, by threads or an event loop.

examples.question: Nginx receives 1,000 requests/min. 70% are static and 30% are proxied to Express. Find static and dynamic requests per minute and per second. Express handles 25 requests/s. Is it enough?
steps: Express capacity = 25 req/s. 25 req/s is greater than 5 req/s, so it is enough. Spare capacity = 25 − 5 = 20 req/s.
examples.answer: Static is 700 req/min (11.7 req/s), dynamic is 300 req/min (5 req/s), and Express is enough, with 20 req/s spare.

total = 1000.0
static_per_min = 0.70 * total
dynamic_per_min = 0.30 * total
static_per_sec = static_per_min / 60
dynamic_per_sec = dynamic_per_min / 60
capacity = 25.0
spare = capacity - dynamic_per_sec
print(f'{static_per_min:.1f}')
print(f'{dynamic_per_min:.1f}')
print(f'{static_per_sec:.1f}')
print(f'{dynamic_per_sec:.1f}')
print(f'{capacity:.1f}')
print(f'{spare:.1f}')

traps: A web server is a role, not always a separate machine. One Node.js process can serve files and run API handlers.
Port 80 is HTTP and port 443 is HTTPS. Ports 3000 and 8080 are common internal app ports, not public web ports.
Static does not mean cached by the browser. Static means the file exists before the request; caching is a separate header decision.
A reverse proxy sits in front of servers for clients. A forward proxy sits in front of clients for servers.
Middleware is not the final handler. It runs before or after the handler and often calls next() to continue.

quiz.q: Name four parts of a browser.
quiz.a: Rendering engine, JavaScript engine, network stack, storage.

quiz.q: Which port is the default for HTTPS?
Why can a web server answer a static file faster than an app server can answer a dynamic request?
quiz.a: It reads a file and sends bytes. No route handler, database query or business logic runs per request.

quiz.q: A web server gets 800 req/min; 60% are static. Find dynamic requests per minute and per second.
Nginx proxies 450 req/min to an app that handles 10 req/s. Is capacity enough? Show the numbers.
quiz.a: 450 ÷ 60 = 7.5 req/s. 10 − 7.5 = 2.5 req/s spare. Yes, capacity is enough.

quiz.q: A Node.js Express app serves both static files and API routes. Does this break the web-server/application-server distinction? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Web server and app server are roles. One Express process can read files from disk and run API handlers. Nginx may still sit in front as a reverse proxy, but the labels describe work, not separate boxes.

quiz.q: Why does the same-origin policy use protocol, host and port, not just host?
quiz.a: Protocol, host and port define an origin. http://a.com:80 and https://a.com:443 can have different trust. The browser treats them as different origins so one cannot read the other's storage or responses without permission.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Nginx, Envoy and HAProxy act as reverse proxies and load balancers in front of many app servers. Kubernetes ingress and cloud API gateways extend the same idea with routing, TLS and rate limits. Serverless functions replace the long-running app server for some workloads, but the request lifecycle remains. Search next for reverse proxy vs API gateway, Node.js event loop and same-origin policy.
